newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - WIN AND 2000.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - WIN AND 2000.

text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN

The presentation on the World Insurance Network given to the London International Insurance and Reinsurance Market Association conference in Dublin last week, was received with considerable scepticism. This may be somewhat worrying to bosses at WIN, for the delegates are the conference represented a chunk of WIN's prime target market.
Concern seems to fall into three main areas.

First, there is a feeling that companies have already sunk millions into other electronic systems such as Limnet and Rinet, and that those investments will be made redundant by WIN unless it is merely a common means of accessing existing systems.
Secondly there is some doubt as to whether or not it can work. Can WIN really become a comprehensive 'one system fits all needs' multi-task operation, or has it spent $12 million to re-invent e-mail.

Thirdly, there is a dilemma involving ownership. Some in the market see the need for a single system around the world adopted by all. The fact that the major broking houses are behind WIN could enable enough clout to be applied to make WIN that system.

But none of the partner brokers has said so far it will make use of WIN compulsory in their operations, and indeed their may be anti-competitive rules in the way if brokers did say to insurers 'you must use WIN'.

And while some see the benefit of a driving force within the industry towards one system, others are concerned about it being run by the brokers, and suggest some third party should have been set up to do it.
WIN has a lot of technical problems to overcome, but it also faces some stiff challenges in changing perceptions among the insurance and reinsurance market.
--oo0oo--

UK life insurer Scottish Widows has highlighted the potential risk to insurance investments which could be caused by the Millennium Bug - the technological issue which could wreck computer systems when the clock ticks over onto the first minute of the year 2000.
The Scottish life company has said it will not buy shares in companies which don't have a strategy to become millennium compliant.
Scottish Widows takes the pragmatic stance that such companies may see their share prices hit if they experience problems on January 1, 2000.
Other insurers are already severing operational links with computer and software suppliers who they think aren't doing enough to get ready for the millennium.
Industry association BIIBA, which represents most leading British insurance brokers, last week lent its weight to the campaign by setting up a Year 2000 Project Team.
BIIBA has set a deadline of December 31, 1998 for all software houses supplying insurance brokers to achieve "demonstrable and tested evidence of compliance."
As BIIBA points out, 2000 is a non-negotiable deadline -- there is no power on earth that could delay it.
